nodes.name: Transmission and distribution equipment suppliers
nodes.mechanism: Flat utility T&D capex at $180B removes annual volume growth for transformers, switchgear, and cable, leaving suppliers with idle capacity.
nodes.logic: These suppliers built capacity expecting rising grid investment for electrification and renewables. A flatline means unit orders stop growing while fixed costs remain, pressuring margins. The effect is direct because utility capex is the primary demand driver for these product categories.
nodes.falsifier: Utilities accelerate replacement of aging equipment within flat capex or storm hardening orders offset new capacity demand.

nodes.name: Aeroderivative gas turbine manufacturers
nodes.mechanism: Data center operators order on-site gas turbines for prime and backup power, creating a new demand stream outside utility capex.
nodes.logic: The need for firm, dispatchable power at data centers bypasses multi-year utility interconnection queues. Order intake for aeroderivative turbines rises even as utility T&D capex stays flat. This is a substitution of behind-the-meter generation for grid supply, so the effect is levered to data center load growth, not linear with utility spending.
nodes.falsifier: Data centers choose fuel cells or wait for grid upgrades if gas permitting and emissions rules make turbines unattractive.

nodes.name: Behind-the-meter solar and storage integrators
nodes.mechanism: Data centers contract for on-site solar arrays and battery storage to lower energy costs and meet sustainability targets, increasing project volume.
nodes.logic: Behind-the-meter projects avoid transmission costs and interconnection queues, making them faster to deploy than grid-connected renewables. Flat utility T&D capex makes grid connection less attractive, pushing more data center energy spend to on-site systems. Each project bundles modules, inverters, and batteries, so integrators see higher unit volume.
nodes.falsifier: High battery costs or limited land at data center sites push buyers toward gas-only solutions.

nodes.name: Rate-regulated electric utilities
nodes.mechanism: Flat T&D capex removes rate base growth, the main driver of allowed revenue under cost-of-service regulation.
nodes.logic: Utilities earn a return on capital invested in transmission and distribution assets. If annual capex is flat and depreciation continues, net rate base growth stalls, limiting revenue and earnings growth. The effect is amplified because utilities had planned rate base growth to support data center load; that load is now served behind the meter.
nodes.falsifier: Utilities win approval for new transmission projects beyond the flat capex baseline, or regulators raise allowed ROE.

nodes.name: Data center operators and developers
nodes.mechanism: Behind-the-meter generation shortens time to power, allowing data centers to bring capacity online faster and avoid grid upgrade costs.
nodes.logic: Utility interconnection queues can delay new data centers by years; on-site gas and solar plus storage bypass those queues. Faster deployment increases the leased or used capacity that drives data center revenue. The benefit is greater for large campuses that can dedicate land and capital to generation.
nodes.falsifier: Utilities impose standby charges or local permits slow on-site generation, erasing the speed advantage.

nodes.name: Behind-the-meter generation economics under standby charges
nodes.mechanism: Utilities file tariff changes adding standby and demand charges to self-generating customers, raising the fixed cost of behind-the-meter generation.
nodes.logic: Regulators may approve charges to prevent cost shifting to remaining ratepayers as data centers defect from the grid. These charges directly reduce the savings that justified on-site generation, lowering project returns and slowing order intake for integrators. The effect is concentrated in jurisdictions with large data center load and utilities facing rate base stagnation.
nodes.falsifier: Commissions reject or cap standby charges because they would discourage beneficial electrification or violate rate design principles.

nodes.name: Diversified electrical equipment suppliers pivoting to data center demand
nodes.mechanism: Grid equipment suppliers reallocate engineering and manufacturing capacity to data center electrical rooms, switchgear, and backup power equipment.
nodes.logic: Flat utility T&D orders push suppliers to chase the fast-growing data center market, which needs similar switchgear, busway, and transformers but through private contracts. Suppliers with broad product lines can offset lost utility volume, though pricing may be more competitive. The response is driven by capacity utilization: factories need volume to cover fixed costs.
nodes.falsifier: Data center equipment specifications require custom designs that utility-focused suppliers cannot meet without costly retooling.

nodes.name: Gas turbine aftermarket service providers
nodes.mechanism: New installed base of aeroderivative turbines drives long-term service agreements, lifting high-margin aftermarket revenue.
nodes.logic: Each on-site turbine requires parts, overhauls, and monitoring over a 20-year life. OEMs respond by expanding field service networks and signing multi-year maintenance contracts. The effect is compounded because data center operators prioritize uptime and prefer OEM service, making aftermarket revenue stickier than equipment sales.
nodes.falsifier: Data centers use third-party maintenance or sign only equipment purchase contracts, suppressing service attach rates.

nodes.name: Project finance for behind-the-meter generation
nodes.mechanism: Debt and equity investors see higher growth in on-site power projects than in flat rate base utilities, lowering the cost of capital for behind-the-meter developers.
nodes.logic: Capital providers reallocate from regulated utility equity to independent power producers, gas turbine lessors, and distributed generation platforms. Cheaper financing improves project returns and accelerates new behind-the-meter buildout. The shift is self-reinforcing as more projects demonstrate bankability.
nodes.falsifier: Lenders view single-customer data center offtake as too concentrated, requiring higher rates or guarantees.

nodes.name: Natural gas pipeline and midstream suppliers
nodes.mechanism: Data center operators with on-site turbines sign firm gas transportation and supply contracts, raising pipeline utilization.
nodes.logic: Behind-the-meter gas turbines need reliable fuel supply, often requiring new laterals or firm capacity on existing pipelines. Midstream companies gain long-term take-or-pay contracts that stabilize revenue. The effect is levered to the number of large data center campuses in gas-producing regions.
nodes.falsifier: Data centers choose dual-fuel turbines or locate where gas is not available, limiting pipeline contract growth.

nodes.name: Behind-the-meter integrator margins
nodes.mechanism: Easier financing attracts more integrators into behind-the-meter solar and storage, competing away project margins.
nodes.logic: As capital floods into the space, new entrants bid aggressively for data center contracts, pressuring equipment and installation pricing. The initial demand growth remains but profit per project shrinks. This margin compression is a typical equilibrium response to an overcapitalized niche.
nodes.falsifier: Specialized engineering or long-term O&M contracts create switching costs that sustain margins despite new entrants.

nodes.name: Data center electrical equipment margins
nodes.mechanism: Many grid equipment suppliers chase the same data center power orders, leading to overcapacity and price competition.
nodes.logic: The pivot to data center demand brings multiple suppliers into a market that previously had fewer competitors. Bidding for hyperscale contracts turns price-driven, squeezing margins despite higher volumes. The effect emerges as lead times shorten and cancellable orders rise.
nodes.falsifier: Data center power demand grows faster than supplier capacity, keeping lead times long and prices firm.

nodes.name: Third-party gas turbine service competition
nodes.mechanism: High aftermarket margins attract independent service providers, competing down service pricing for aeroderivative turbines.
nodes.logic: As the installed base of on-site turbines grows, independent firms offer parts and overhaul services at lower cost. OEMs may be forced to discount long-term service agreements to retain share. The effect is most visible in regions with many small turbines where third-party logistics are easier.
nodes.falsifier: Proprietary parts, software locks, and data center uptime requirements keep service captive to OEMs.

nodes.name: Utility revenue from standby and backup service
nodes.mechanism: Standby charges and grid connection fees create a new recurring revenue stream for utilities serving self-generating data centers.
nodes.logic: Even as data centers install on-site generation, they often retain a grid connection for backup and export. Utilities earn monthly demand charges and standby fees that partly offset lost volumetric revenue. This new fixed revenue reduces the earnings hit from flat rate base, though it may be contested in rate cases.
nodes.falsifier: Data centers disconnect entirely or install enough on-site redundancy to avoid grid standby charges.

trigger.actor: US data center operators and developers
trigger.action: meet new load growth with behind-the-meter on-site gas turbines and solar plus storage rather than grid-supplied power
trigger.magnitude: US grid capital expenditure flatlines near $180 billion annually through 2030; utility transmission and distribution capex growth remains below 1 percent annually
trigger.reversibility: Could be reversed if data center operators return to grid purchases due to lower utility rates, stricter emissions limits on on-site gas, or utility rate reforms that accelerate grid interconnection.

reactions.incentive: Protect rate base growth and recover fixed grid costs as large customers self-generate
reactions.likelyResponse: File standby and demand charge tariff revisions with state commissions to impose fixed charges on self-generating customers

reactions.incentive: Maintain factory utilization and revenue as utility T&D orders flatten
reactions.likelyResponse: Shift engineering and manufacturing capacity toward data center power equipment, industrial electrification, and export markets

reactions.incentive: Accelerate time to power and lock in lower energy costs outside the grid queue
reactions.likelyResponse: Sign long-term supply and service agreements for on-site gas turbines, solar, storage, and firm gas transportation

reactions.actor: Gas turbine and on-site power equipment manufacturers
reactions.incentive: Capture new demand and convert it into recurring service revenue
reactions.likelyResponse: Expand production capacity for aeroderivative turbines and sign multi-year maintenance agreements

reactions.incentive: Allocate debt and equity to faster-growing energy infrastructure than flat rate base utilities
reactions.likelyResponse: Reduce valuation premia for regulated utilities and increase financing for behind-the-meter generation projects and gas turbine leasing
